newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Defections focus Seoul minds on crisis management.
newsitem.headline: Defections focus Seoul minds on crisis management.

text.p: The defection of a family of 17 North Koreans and a submarine scare has focused South Korean minds on crisis management after fruitless attempts at inter-Korean detente.
Both incidents struck to the heart of worries that a collapsing North Korea could spill refugees across its borders and decide on a pyrrhic last gasp attack on its capitalist rival.
Suddenly, no one on either side seems in the mood to talk and many South Koreans are losing hope in the prospect of a peaceful reunification of a nation split apart by the 1950-53 Korean War.

The public is crying for stiffened defences against what it regards as the communist menace to the north. Politicians are calling for a more realistic attitude to handle any surge of defections from the impoverished and hunger-hit North Korea.
A family of 17, the biggest group of North Korean defectors since the war, arrived in Seoul on Monday, six weeks after launching an epic escape through China and Hong Kong.
South Korean President Kim Young-sam, entering the last year of his single term in office, has veered from hawkish to dovish on North Korea.
His current rigid hardline stand is finding a sympathetic audience in an electorate feeling vulnerable to what could happen next in North Korea.

After deflecting criticism of the military's slack handling of a submarine incursion in September with a sweeping reshuffle of military top brass, he has now ordered his generals to tighten discipline among the rank and file.
Raw recruits on compulsory military service have been banned from using civilian-style beepers, flashing credit cards on bases and listening to radios on duty.
A drive is also on to upgrade defences.
On Tuesday, the Defence Ministry announced major rises in spending over the five years until 2002, with an average 12.9 per cent increase each year.
The ministry said much of the extra spending would go on early warning systems and intelligence gathering, key to both heading off an attack and preparing the nation for a refugee stream.
"The budget will be spent over the five years starting in 1998 to improve the nation's defence capabilities," a statement said.
"The defence programme for 1998-2002 is aimed at maintaining peace by deterring wars with North Korea and neighbouring countries," it added.

The measures all add up to a radical reassessment of the North Korean threat -- from a nation that should be feared for its military prowess to a nation that should be feared for what poverty could drive it to do.

The Ministry for National Reunification, long dedicated to working towards Korean union, has shifted its focus from managing dialogue and contacts to working out how to handle the consequences of North Korea cracking up.
On the drawing board is a plan for a new ministry bureau to deal exclusively with North Korean refugees tentatively named the Bureau of Humanitarian Assistance.
At the same time, the Office of South-North Dialogue would be cut back.
Still the government hasn't lost all hope for a merger of the two Koreas.

At a cabinet level meeting on Tuesday, ministers approved a plan to send 20 officials to China, Germany, Vietnam and former East European countries to study how they handled the change from communism.
None of these changes is fast enough for South Korean politicians.

Parliamentarians earlier this week attacked a government proposed bill named the "Act for the Protection of North Korean Escapees" as inadequate, singling out the lack of preparations to cope with a refugee exodus.

"Things have changed a lot since the bill was drawn up," said ruling New Korea Party member Lee Man-sup. "Now that a massive exodus of North Korean people into the South is expected, the bill needs modification."
